stories.title: Ye Xian
stories.tradition: Chinese (set among non-Han southern peoples; informant described as Zhuang)
stories.atuNote: Ting's index places the fish-helper tale under 510A (per Wikipedia citing Ting); confirm in Ting 1978
stories.dateSource: Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang by Duan Chengshi; sources give c. 850 or c. 860
stories.form: literary record of an oral tale
stories.summary: A girl mistreated by her stepmother befriends a golden-eyed fish. After the stepmother kills it, a spirit tells her to keep its bones, which grant wishes. She attends a festival in splendid clothes, loses a golden slipper, and the king who obtains it searches for its owner and marries her.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her stepmother and half-sister force her into servitude and kill the fish she befriends.
The bones of the fish grant her wishes, including the clothes she wears to the festival.
A golden slipper left behind at the festival reaches the king, who has every maiden try it; it fits only her.
The servant girl becomes the king's wife.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ye Xian (overview, plot, tale-type note)
Beauchamp, Asian Origins of Cinderella (Oral Tradition journal)

stories.title: Kongjwi and Patjwi
stories.atuNote: Shares similarities with ATU 510 but has its own Korean type KT 450
stories.dateSource: Source says it was passed down orally for generations before first being recorded; first-record date not given
stories.summary: Kongjwi is abused by her stepmother and stepsister Patjwi and is helped by animals and supernatural helpers. She marries a magistrate, but unlike Western Cinderella tales the story continues: Patjwi drowns her and takes her place, Kongjwi is reborn in other forms, and her husband learns the truth.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her stepmother and Patjwi abuse and overwork her.
A cow, a toad, birds and a fairy help her in widely told versions.
NEEDS SOURCE: lost-shoe recognition appears in our team's notes but was not confirmed in retrieved sources.
NEEDS SOURCE: difficult household tasks appear in our team's notes but were not confirmed in retrieved sources.
After Patjwi drowns her, Kongjwi is reborn as a lotus flower and then as a marble.
She is killed by Patjwi and returns in other forms to reveal the truth.
She marries the magistrate.

stories.title: Tam and Cam
stories.atuNote: Not confirmed in a retrieved source as an ATU assignment
stories.dateSource: Landes, Saigon 1886, described as the earliest European transcription
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest transcription we located, not necessarily the earliest record; many Vietnamese variants existed
stories.summary: Tam is mistreated by her stepmother and half-sister Cam, who steals her catch of fish. A spirit tells her to bury the bones of her fish, which help her. A magical slipper leads a king to marry her, but she is killed and reincarnated several times before regaining her place.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her stepmother makes her do all the housework, and Cam steals her catch.
A spirit tells her to bury the fish's bones in pots at the corners of her bed, and they help her.
A slipper reaches the sovereign, who says he will marry the girl it fits; it fits Tam.
After being killed, she is reincarnated as a bird, a loom and a gold apple.
She is killed by her stepmother and sister and returns in new forms.
She becomes the sovereign's wife.

stories.title: Vasilisa the Beautiful
stories.atuNote: Haney: AT 480B*; Russian scholarship: SUS 480B* 'Stepmother and Stepdaughter'. NOT a 510A tale.
stories.dateSource: Collected by Afanasyev in Narodnye russkie skazki
stories.summary: Vasilisa's dying mother leaves her a magic doll. Her stepmother sends her to Baba Yaga's hut for fire. With the doll's help she completes Baba Yaga's tasks and returns with a skull lantern whose fire destroys her stepfamily.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her stepmother sends her into the forest hoping Baba Yaga will devour her.
A doll given by her dying mother guides her and does the work.
Baba Yaga sets her tasks, which she completes with the doll's help.
She ends the tale married into the royal household.

stories.title: Shakuntala (Kalidasa's play)
stories.tradition: Sanskrit literary drama adapting a Mahabharata episode
stories.atuNote: Not a Cinderella-type tale. Display as a thematic parallel only.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: Mahabharata episode: epic composed roughly 400 BCE-400 CE; Kalidasa's play: c. 4th-5th century CE (date uncertain)
stories.dateCaveat: The curse and the signet ring are Kalidasa's additions; they are not in the Mahabharata version
stories.summary: In Kalidasa's play, King Dushyanta marries Shakuntala and leaves her his signet ring. A sage's curse makes him forget her. The ring is lost in a river, he rejects her, and only when the ring is recovered does his memory return, leading to their reunion.

motifEntries.howItAppears: The signet ring is the token that lifts the curse once he sees it again. (Kalidasa's version only.)
Dushyanta repudiates her under the curse, and they are reunited after the ring is found.
She is the child of a celestial mother, Menaka, and is protected by birds in the wilderness (the source of her name).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Shakuntala
NIOS: Abhijnanashakuntalam chapter (source and additions)

stories.title: Cupid and Psyche
stories.region: Roman Empire (author a North African native)
stories.tradition: Latin literary tale within Apuleius's novel
stories.atuNote: Sources differ; sometimes 'Search for the Lost Husband'
stories.dateCaveat: Eros and Psyche appear in Greek art from the 4th century BCE; Apuleius gives the only surviving extended ancient narrative
stories.summary: Venus is jealous of the mortal Psyche and sends Cupid to punish her, but he falls in love and meets her in secret. When Psyche's curiosity breaks his trust, he leaves. Venus sets her four tasks, including a trip to the underworld, and Psyche is finally made immortal and reunited with Cupid.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Ants sort the seeds, a reed advises her, Jupiter's eagle fetches the water, and a tower tells her how to enter the underworld.
Venus assigns four seemingly impossible tasks, the last a journey to Proserpina in the underworld.
Psyche's curiosity separates her from Cupid; after her trials they are reunited and she becomes immortal.

stories.title: The Tale of Two Brothers
stories.atuNote: Wikipedia notes the tale mixes several types and ATU fits it poorly
stories.dateSource: British Museum dating of Papyrus d'Orbiney; other sources give c. 1197-1185 BCE (reign of Seti II)
stories.dateCaveat: The only known copy; the museum says it is probably roughly contemporary with composition
stories.summary: Bata is falsely accused by his brother Anubis's wife and forced to leave. The brothers are later reunited after Anubis learns the truth. Gods fashion a wife for Bata, who betrays him; he is killed, returns in other forms, is reborn as her son, and becomes king.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Bata appears in other forms, including a bull, before his rebirth.
Bata is reborn as the son of the woman who betrayed him and becomes king of Egypt.
Anubis drives Bata away on his wife's false claim, then discovers the truth and the brothers are reunited.

He steals fire back from Zeus in a fennel stalk and returns it to humans.

stories.title: Raven Steals the Light
stories.region: Pacific Northwest Coast (Haida, Tlingit and neighbouring nations)
stories.dateSource: Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905); Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
stories.dateCaveat: A living oral tradition far older than its first written record. Versions differ by nation and storyteller.
stories.form: oral tradition recorded by an ethnologist
stories.summary: In a dark world, Raven learns that light is hidden in a distant house. He turns himself into a speck of dirt, slips into the water the owner's daughter drinks, is born as her child, and tricks the grandfather into opening the box, releasing light into the world.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Raven uses disguise and persuasion to get past the guardian of the light.
He gets the light out of its box and releases it, becoming the sun and stars.
He turns himself into a speck of dirt to slip into the daughter's drinking water.

Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (Project Gutenberg)

stories.title: Maui obtains fire from Mahuika
stories.region: Aotearoa New Zealand (Maori; Maui stories are Polynesia-wide)
stories.dateSource: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (drawing on manuscripts by Te Rangikaheke)
stories.dateCaveat: Oral tradition much older. Maui stories vary across Polynesia.
stories.summary: Maui finds that fire has been lost and goes to Mahuika, the fire goddess. He tricks her into giving him her burning fingernails one by one, extinguishing each, until she angrily hurls the last, and fire lodges in certain trees.

motifEntries.howItAppears: He tricks Mahuika into giving up her fingernails of fire by making excuses after extinguishing each.
He obtains fire from Mahuika by trickery; in some traditions the fire is stored in trees.
Maui is born prematurely and thrown into the sea wrapped in a tress of his mother's topknot.

stories.title: Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh
stories.dateSource: Britannica: K'iche' text in Latin script; original lost; earliest surviving copy by Ximenez 1701-1703
stories.dateCaveat: Text was surely written in hieroglyphs before the Conquest (UNC Libraries); sources also say the Hero Twins appear on Classic-period ceramics
stories.form: written, from older oral and hieroglyphic tradition
stories.summary: The twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque are summoned to the underworld Xibalba, as their father and uncle were before them. They defeat the Lords of Death through cunning, and are said to become the Sun and Moon (or Venus).

motifEntries.howItAppears: They overcome the Lords of Xibalba through cunning and trickery.
They are transformed into celestial bodies, interpreted as the Sun and Moon.
Their father is killed in Xibalba and the twins defeat death there. NEEDS SOURCE: confirm the twins' own death and resurrection in Tedlock or Christenson.
Their mother Xquic conceives when the skull of One Hunahpu spits into her hand.

stories.title: Anansi buys the Sky God's stories
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest located record, not earliest. Oral tradition is older. Retellings differ on which beings Nyame demands.
stories.form: oral tradition recorded by an ethnographer
stories.summary: All stories belong to Nyame, the Sky God. Anansi offers to buy them, and Nyame names a price of dangerous creatures, such as the python Onini, the leopard Osebo and the hornets Mmoboro (and the fairy Mmoatia in some versions). Anansi captures each by trickery, and the stories become 'spider stories.'

motifEntries.howItAppears: He captures the creatures through traps and ruses, such as a pit for the leopard and a gourd for the hornets.
Nyame sets his price as capturing creatures no one else could take.

sources.title: Mythlok: The Theft of Stories (secondary; cites Rattray 1930)
Courlander retelling, 'All Stories Are Anansi's' (school page; secondary)

stories.sensitivity: Rattray was a colonial-era ethnographer. Credit the Akan tradition and look for Ghanaian-authored retellings.

stories.summary: A bamboo cutter finds a baby in a glowing bamboo stalk and raises her as Kaguya-hime. When five suitors seek her hand, she sets each an impossible task. All fail, she refuses even the emperor, and she is finally revealed to be from the Moon and returns there.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Kaguya-hime assigns five suitors tasks that cannot be fulfilled, such as finding the Buddha's stone begging bowl.
She is found as a baby inside a glowing bamboo stalk and is later revealed to be from the Moon.
